goldens.comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

findings.blocking_reason: Fire-and-forget async forEach drops deleteEvent/deleteMeeting promises during reschedule, silently losing errors and potentially leaving orphaned calendar events — a correctness regression in production-running code.
findings.body: the property does NOT hold. The `try { bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) } catch` pattern at `reschedule.ts:124-139` is a regression: `forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` promises are dropped (fire-and-forget) and their rejections escape as unhandled promise rejections that the surrounding try/catch cannot catch. findings.blocking_reason: Confirmed regression: main used map(async)+Promise.all to await external calendar/video deletes, but PR replaced it with forEach(async) which discards promises, causing fire-and-forget deletes, swallowed errors, and external state divergence from DB.
findings.body:
The PR's mechanical refactor of "add `await` to `getCalendar()` / `appStore[key]` calls" was applied inside `forEach(async ...)` callbacks where the await is semantically void — `Array.prototype.forEach` discards returned promises, so the awaited operations run in the microtask queue with no caller able to observe their completion or rejection. This is a SYSTEMIC control gap, not three isolated bugs. Four affected call sites span the ENTIRE booking-lifecycle surface (cancel + reschedule + tRPC reschedule):

(a) `packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts:124-134` — REGRESSION. Main used `bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...) -> await Promise.all(promises)`. PR-review replaced with `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` inside a `try/catch`. The try/catch cannot catch async rejections (promise is discarded before the throw propagates), `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` (line ~143) fires before calendar/video deletes complete, and any `deleteEvent` failure is silently swallowed. External calendar/video state diverges from DB state (ghost events).

(b) `packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts:124-134` — REGRESSION, byte-identical pattern to (a).

(c) `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts:458-470` — NEW RACE. `forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)) })` populates `apiDeletes` asynchronously in the microtask queue. `apiDeletes` is awaited at line 617 (`await apiDeletes`) and line 652 (`Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`); at both awaits the array may be empty or partial because the forEach callbacks have not yet run to completion. Main does not exhibit this pattern.

(d) `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx:553` — UNFLAGGED 4th instance. tRPC `reschedule` mutation: `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` with no `Promise.all`, immediately followed by `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` at line 570. PR diff confirmed: changed `forEach((bookingRef) =>` -> `forEach(async (bookingRef) =>` and `getCalendar(...)` -> `await getCalendar(...)`. (On main, `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/` is a directory of handler files, not a single `bookings.tsx`; PR consolidated/relocated this code, so the regression baseline is ambiguous — but the PR-introduced `forEach(async ...)` pattern is confirmed and structurally identical to (a)/(b).)

Compound effect: across all four paths, external calendar/video deletes are silently fire-and-forget; `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and the final DB transaction proceed before external deletes complete; a `deleteEvent` rejection cannot be caught by any caller. The PR appears correct to a grep-based review (`await` keywords present) but the awaits are structurally disconnected from control flow. This is the same root mechanism as the PR's broader "eager `import()` with no try/catch" surface — async work is kicked off but not joined — except here it directly mutates external calendar state.

Repo-wide `forEach(async` survey on the PR branch: 14 matches in 7 files. The 4 booking-flow-critical instances are (a)-(d) above; other matches in `workflows.tsx`, `reminderScheduler.ts`, `nodeScheduler.ts` are not all PR-introduced and not all booking-flow critical, but the pattern should be audited repo-wide.
findings.evidence: vital/lib/reschedule.ts:124-134 (PR): `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { if (bookingRef.uid) { if (bookingRef.type.endsWith("_calendar")) { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); } else if (bookingRef.type.endsWith("_video")) { return deleteMeeting(...); } } });` — no `Promise.all`, no `await` on the forEach result (impossible). Compare main: `const promises = bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }); try { await Promise.all(promises); } catch (error) {...}`. wipemycalother identical. handleCancelBooking.ts:458-470 `forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)) })` with `apiDeletes` awaited at 617 and 652. bookings.tsx:553 same `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })`, PR diff hunk confirms `forEach((bookingRef) =>` -> `forEach(async (bookingRef) =>` and `getCalendar(` -> `await getCalendar(`. `forEach(async` survey: `rg "forEach\\(async" --type ts --type tsx` -> 14 matches across 7 files; 4 in booking-flow paths.
findings.title: COMPOUND: Systemic fire-and-forget control gap across booking lifecycle — mechanical `await` refactor inside `forEach(async ...)` disconnected from control flow in 4 call sites (2 confirmed regressions, 1 new race, 1 unflagged instance)

findings.blocking_reason: This is a performance optimization suggestion about eager vs lazy loading; the code functions correctly and introduces no correctness, security, or contract regression.
findings.body:
The PR title says "async imports of all apps", and the implementation matches that literally — but the semantics deserve a flag because the change is **not** an on-demand lazy-loading refactor, and on the server runtime it is **strictly more expensive** than the static imports it replaced.

**How the code evaluates.** `appStore` is an object literal. In JavaScript, object literal property values are evaluated eagerly at construction time. Each `import("./applecalendar")` (etc.) is a runtime expression that returns a `Promise<Module>` and initiates the dynamic import immediately. So the moment any consumer first imports `@calcom/app-store`, the module body runs, the object literal is constructed, and **all 28 `import()` calls fire in parallel** — before any consumer has called `await appStore[key]`. This is "parallel-imports-of-everything", not "import-on-first-use".

**Server runtime cost (Node, where all 5 consumers run).** The 5 consumers (`packages/core/videoClient.ts:26`, `packages/lib/payment/handlePayment.ts:26`, `packages/lib/payment/deletePayment.ts:16`, `packages/app-store/_utils/getCalendar.ts:15`, `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts:589`) are all server-side booking-flow code. Under Node, a static `import * as x from "./x"` is resolved at build time and the module is in the same bundle — zero runtime I/O. A dynamic `import("./x")` at runtime triggers Node's module loader: path resolution + `fs.readFile` + parse + compile per chunk. 28 parallel dynamic imports at startup therefore issue 28 concurrent filesystem reads (plus per-chunk resolution) where the old code issued **zero** runtime I/O. The PR trades a build-time cost (bundling) for a runtime cost (28 async fs reads at first import). For a serverless/edge deploy, this is even sharper: each cold start fetches 28 chunks over the network in parallel instead of loading one bundle.

**Bundle-splitting benefit is partially defeated.** Dynamic `import()` is the canonical tool for code splitting — each app becomes its own chunk that loads on demand. But because the object literal eagerly invokes every `import()`, **every chunk is requested on first import of `app-store`**, regardless of whether the booking flow needs stripepayment or googlecalendar or zoomvideo. The split chunks still load — all of them, at once. The only retained benefit is that the chunks are cached by the module system after first resolution, so a *subsequent* server warm path pays nothing. The first-request cost, though, is worse than the static-import baseline it replaced.

**Tree-shaking.** Per-chunk tree-shaking is preserved (each app chunk is independently DCE'd). But whole-program tree-shaking of unused apps is **weakened**: with static imports, a bundler could in principle prove which `appStore[key]` accesses happen and DCE unused app modules. With dynamic `import()`, the access key is a runtime string (`dirName`, `calendarType.split("_").join("")`, `appName`), so the bundler must conservatively retain every app chunk. In practice cal.com ships all 28 apps anyway, so this is a theoretical regression, not a measured one — but it is a real change in the bundler's optimization ceiling.

**Re-import safety (verified safe).** ES module semantics memoize modules: the `app-store/index.ts` body runs exactly once per bundle. Re-importing `@calcom/app-store` from any of the 5 consumer files returns the cached module namespace — the same `appStore` object with the same 28 already-created (resolved or pending) Promise objects. `await appStore[key]` on a re-import awaits the same promise; it does **not** re-fire `import()`. I traced all 5 consumers and confirmed each does a single `import appStore from "@calcom/app-store"` at the top of the file and then `await appStore[key]` inside a function body — no consumer re-imports expecting fresh loads, and the module system would not honor that expectation anyway. This sub-question is clean.

**Why this is `important` and not `critical`.** The code will not crash or produce wrong results from eagerness alone — the promises resolve and the module system memoizes them correctly. The cost is a latent performance regression on cold starts (server: 28 parallel fs reads; edge: 28 parallel network fetches) that is **strictly worse** than the static-import baseline, plus a weakening of the bundler's ability to drop unused apps. Given the PR's stated intent ("async imports of all apps"), this may be an intentional stepping stone toward a future lazy refactor — but as shipped, the runtime cost trade is negative on the server path that all 5 consumers exercise.
findings.dimension_name: Eager vs Lazy Import Semantics & Runtime Cost
findings.evidence: Step 1: Any consumer (e.g. `packages/core/videoClient.ts:4` `import appStore from "@calcom/app-store"`) imports the module. Step 2: The module body of `packages/app-store/index.ts` runs, constructing the object literal on lines 1–31. Step 3: JS object-literal evaluation evaluates each property value eagerly, so `import("./applecalendar")` (line 3), `import("./caldavcalendar")` (line 4), … `import("./sylapsvideo")` (line 30) each execute and return a Promise that has *already begun* the dynamic import. All 28 promises are in-flight before the object literal finishes constructing. Step 4: `export default appStore` (line 33) hands consumers an object whose values are pending Promises. Step 5: Consumer calls `await appStore[appName as keyof typeof appStore]` (`videoClient.ts:26`) — this awaits an already-in-flight promise rather than initiating a fresh import. Step 6: Re-import of `@calcom/app-store` by a second consumer (e.g. `handlePayment.ts:3`) returns the memoized module namespace per ES module spec — the same `appStore` object, the same 28 Promises — so no `import()` re-fires. Verified all 5 consumers (`videoClient.ts`, `handlePayment.ts`, `deletePayment.ts`, `getCalendar.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts`) follow this single-import + `await appStore[key]` pattern.
findings.suggestion: If the intent was lazy on-demand loading, convert the object literal to a function/thunk so imports fire on first access: `const appStore = { applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar"), ... }` and have consumers do `const mod = await appStore[key]()`. This preserves per-app code splitting and only fetches the chunk actually needed. If the intent really is "load all 28 in parallel at startup", keep the current shape but document the cold-start cost in a comment, and consider pre-`await`-ing with `Promise.all` at a controlled init point (e.g. server warmup) rather than implicitly at first import — that makes the cost explicit and measurable. Either way, add a brief comment above the object literal stating which semantics is intended so future readers don't misread `import()` inside an object literal as lazy.
findings.title: Object literal eagerly fires all 28 `import()` promises at module init — not lazy on-demand loading; runtime cost on server/edge is higher than the static imports it replaced

findings.blocking_reason: forEach(async ...) drops promises so errors escape the try/catch as unhandled rejections and the function returns true before deletions complete, a regression of the error-handling and cancellation semantics that worked before.
findings.body:
CHANGED END (reschedule.ts:124-139): a `try { bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); ... return deleteMeeting(...); }) } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` block. The try/catch wraps the `forEach` call, intending to catch errors from getCalendar/deleteEvent/deleteMeeting.

OTHER END (_utils/getCalendar.ts:9): `export const getCalendar = async (credential): Promise<Calendar | null> => { ... await appStore[...] ... }`. getCalendar is async — it awaits an appStore lookup and can reject. deleteMeeting (from @calcom/core/videoClient) likewise returns a promise. The surrounding try/catch assumes these calls are awaited within its protected region.

DISAGREEMENT: `Array.prototype.forEach` does NOT await async callbacks. forEach invokes the async callback synchronously, ignores the returned promise, and returns immediately. Consequences: (a) The `return calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` / `return deleteMeeting(...)` inside the async callback are dropped — the deleteEvent/deleteMeeting promises are fire-and-forget, so the calendar event / video meeting deletions are never awaited and may not complete before the function returns `true` at line 151 (callers believe cancellation succeeded). (b) Any rejection from `await getCalendar(...)` or `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` occurs in a microtask AFTER forEach has returned synchronously, so it becomes an unhandled promise rejection that the `try/catch` at lines 124/135 cannot catch — the `logger.error(error.message)` handler is never reached for these errors. Before getCalendar became async, synchronous exceptions from it were caught by the try/catch; after the refactor those failures now escape as unhandled rejections (in Node, process-level 'unhandledRejection' / crash). The two ends disagree: the try/catch assumes awaited semantics, but forEach provides fire-and-forget semantics. This is a regression, not intentional — nothing awaits the forEach or collects the returned promises.
findings.title: forEach(async ...) drops deleteEvent/deleteMeeting promises and their rejections escape the try/catch as unhandled promise rejections

findings.blocking_reason: Regression: replacing await Promise.allSettled with forEach(async) silently discards deletion failures and breaks ordering invariants that worked before this PR.
findings.body: Pre-PR code used `await Promise.allSettled(map(async))` (no try/catch needed). Post-PR code uses `forEach(async)` with NO try/catch at all. This is the worst site. It breaks two invariants: 1. Ordering: Pre-PR awaited all calendar/video deletions before sending webhooks. Post-PR `forEach` returns synchronously → webhooks fire while old calendar events may still exist. 2. Error observability: Pre-PR `allSettled` captured rejections. Post-PR `forEach` discards all returned promises → deletion failures are entirely silent. Root cause: `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await its async callback.
findings.title: Regression from Promise.allSettled to forEach(async) with no try/catch causes silent deletion failures

findings.body: Pre-PR code used `await Promise.all(map(async))` with try/catch. Post-PR code uses `forEach(async)` with ineffective try/catch. This breaks two invariants: 1. Ordering: Pre-PR awaited all calendar/video deletions before sending the reschedule email. Post-PR `forEach` returns synchronously → email fires while old calendar events may still exist on the user's Google/Outlook calendar. 2. Error observability: Pre-PR `Promise.all` captured rejections (logged via try/catch). Post-PR `forEach` discards all returned promises → rejections become unhandled rejections that the try/catch cannot catch. Root cause: `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await its async callback.

findings.blocking_reason: The forEach(async) pattern drops calendar delete promises, causing the API to report successful cancellation while external calendar events may silently fail to delete — creating inconsistent production state between the app and external calendars.
findings.body: The recurringEvent cancellation branch (lines 458-470) iterates credentials with `forEach(async (credential) => {...})`. Array.prototype.forEach does NOT await its async callback, so the callback's promise is discarded (fire-and-forget). Inside the callback, `await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` is awaited and its RESOLVED VALUE (not the promise) is pushed to `apiDeletes` (line 467: `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)` where `deletedEvent` is the awaited result). This differs from every other branch: the else branch at line 472 pushes the un-awaited PROMISE (`apiDeletes.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(...) as Promise<unknown>)`), the legacy for...of branch at line 482 does the same, and the video branches at lines 500/509 push promises. The enclosing handler later awaits `apiDeletes` at line 617 (`await apiDeletes;`) and line 652 (`await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes));`). Because the recurringEvent branch pushes resolved values (and does so asynchronously, after forEach returns synchronously), those awaits see either an empty array or an array of non-promise values — they resolve immediately WITHOUT waiting for the calendar deleteEvent operations to complete. Concrete consequence: for recurringEvent cancellations, the HTTP response is sent (line 656-657 / 618-619) before external calendar events are actually deleted; deleteEvent failures (including getCalendar rejections inside the async callback) are completely unhandled — no try/catch wraps the forEach, and the rejected async-callback promise is dropped, surfacing as an unhandled rejection. Recurring event cancellations can silently fail to delete external calendar events while the API reports success.
findings.title: forEach(async) drops calendar delete promises in recurringEvent cancellation; await apiDeletes cannot wait for them

findings.blocking_reason: The PR actually improves behavior (old code silently never called deleteEvent), and the remaining fire-and-forget race is a transient correctness concern, not data corruption or a regression of working behavior.
findings.body:
The PR converts `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` and adds `await getCalendar(...)` inside the callback. `Array.prototype.forEach` does **not** await the returned promise from an async callback — it returns immediately after scheduling each iteration. This means:

1. **Errors are silently swallowed**: `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` returns a `Promise`. If `deleteEvent` rejects (e.g. Google Calendar API error, expired OAuth token, network failure), the rejection propagates into the async callback's returned promise, which nobody awaits. This becomes an unhandled promise rejection — no log, no retry, no surface to the user. The reschedule flow reports success even though calendar event deletion failed.

2. **Race condition with downstream steps**: The code immediately after the forEach proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` (line 570), builds `evt` (line 574), fires `BOOKING_CANCELLED` webhooks (line 599-618), and the caller continues to create the new booking. The `deleteEvent` calls (which now actually execute, unlike before — see below) run concurrently with all of this. The old calendar event may still exist when the new booking is created, causing transient double-booked slots on the user's calendar.

3. **Pre-existing silent no-op is partially fixed but not fully**: Before this PR, `getCalendar(...)` already returned `Promise<Calendar | null>` (see `packages/app-store/_utils/getCalendar.ts:9` — it is declared `async`). The old code `const calendar = getCalendar(...)` bound `calendar` to a **Promise object**, which has no `deleteEvent` property, so `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` was `undefined?.(...)` — a silent no-op. The `await` added by this PR correctly retrieves the `Calendar` instance so `deleteEvent` is now actually invoked. This is a real improvement, but because the surrounding `forEach` still doesn't await, the fix is incomplete: the deletion runs but its outcome is unobservable.

The PR narrative calls the `forEach(async ...)` pattern "cosmetic" — but for this specific call site it is more than cosmetic. It is the difference between `deleteEvent` never running (old behavior) and `deleteEvent` running with unhandled rejection risk and ordering hazards (new behavior).
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `bookingsRouter` `reschedule` handler (line 530+) reaches line 553 `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})`.
Step 2: `forEach` invokes the async callback for each `bookingRef`; each callback returns a Promise that `forEach` discards (MDN: "forEach does not wait for promises").
Step 3: Inside the callback at line 556, `await getCalendar(credentialsMap.get(bookingRef.type))` resolves to a `Calendar` instance (getCalendar is declared `async` in `packages/app-store/_utils/getCalendar.ts:9`, returns `Promise<Calendar | null>`).
Step 4: `return calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` (line 558) invokes `deleteEvent`, which returns a Promise. That Promise is returned from the async callback, which is discarded by `forEach`.
Step 5: Control flow immediately continues at line 570 `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` without waiting for `deleteEvent` to settle. If `deleteEvent` rejects, the rejection is unhandled.
Step 6: Pre-PR, `calendar` was the Promise object itself (no `await`), so `calendar?.deleteEvent` was `undefined` and `deleteEvent` was never called — confirming the PR changes runtime behavior here from silent no-op to fire-and-forget real call.
findings.title: forEach(async ...) makes deleteEvent fire-and-forget — errors silently lost and race with downstream reschedule steps

findings.blocking_reason: The PR replaces static imports with a dynamic import, introducing a new runtime failure mode (chunk-load failure) that can crash booking creation after the booking is already persisted, leaving orphaned records — a concrete behavioral regression.
findings.body:
Line 26 changed `appStore[key]` to `await appStore[key]`, introducing a runtime chunk-load failure mode that did not exist with static imports. There is no try/catch around this await, and the two callers in `handleNewBooking.ts` (lines 1411 and 1891) also have no try/catch around the `handlePayment` call. The surrounding try/catch blocks in `handleNewBooking.ts` (line 315 for conflict checking, line 534 for timeOutOfBounds) do not cover these call sites.

If the `stripepayment` chunk fails to load at runtime (CDN issues, ad blockers, network errors, cache miss), `await appStore[key]` throws an unhandled rejection that propagates through `handlePayment` → `handleNewBooking` → tRPC handler → HTTP 500. The booking has already been created in the database at this point, so the user is left with an orphaned, unpaid booking record and an opaque server error.

With static imports, the module was either available at runtime or the build failed — no runtime crash path existed. This is a behavioral regression introduced by the PR.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the `await appStore[key]` on line 26 in a try/catch. On import failure, either return `null` (matching the existing null-check path that skips payment creation gracefully) or throw a typed error that the caller can catch and handle. At minimum, coordinate with the `handleNewBooking.ts` call sites (lines 1411, 1891) to add try/catch handling that logs the import failure and either continues without payment or rolls back the booking.
findings.title: Unhandled dynamic import failure crashes booking creation

findings.blocking_reason: Unhandled promise rejection risk is a defensive programming concern; the finding does not concretely demonstrate a reachable production crash or data loss.
findings.body: bookings.tsx:553 forEach(async) has NO try/catch (unlike vital) + async getCalendar = unhandled promise rejection in tRPC resolver on any calendar/chunk error, risking process crash or opaque 500.

findings.blocking_reason: The async getCalendar refactor inside forEach(async...) causes apiDeletes to be awaited while still empty in handleCancelBooking.ts, a behavioral regression where external calendar deletes are no longer initiated before the DB status flip and email send.
findings.body:
The PR's core refactor converts `getCalendar` from synchronous to async (dynamic `import()` of app-store chunks). To accommodate this, every iteration callback that previously called `getCalendar(...)` synchronously now does `await getCalendar(...)` inside a `forEach(async ...)`. This introduces a shared mechanism across all three flagged sites that is worse than each individual `forEach(async)` bug suggests:

1. In `vital/lib/reschedule.ts` (lines 125-134) and `wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts` (lines 125-134), the callback was already `forEach` on `main` (so the deletes were already fire-and-forget), BUT on `main` the callback was synchronous: `getCalendar(...)` returned immediately and `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` was *initiated* synchronously during the `forEach` pass, before `sendRequestRescheduleEmail()` ran on line 143. After the PR, `await getCalendar(...)` suspends the callback, so `deleteEvent` is not even *called* until the dynamic import resolves — which happens AFTER `forEach` returns synchronously and AFTER `sendRequestRescheduleEmail()` fires. The PR therefore widened the race window from 'email fires before delete completes' (pre-existing) to 'email fires before delete is even initiated' (new). The individual findings frame this as a regression from `.map()`+`Promise.all`, but the diff patch shows `main` already used `forEach`; the actual PR-introduced harm is the `await getCalendar` deferral inside the discarded async callback.

2. In `handleCancelBooking.ts` (lines 458-470), the PR added `await getCalendar(credential)` inside `forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })`. Because the callback now suspends at `await getCalendar`, the `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)` calls happen in the microtask queue, after `forEach` returns. `apiDeletes` is then `await`ed at line 617 (`await apiDeletes`) and line 652 (`Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`), but at those points the array is empty or only partially populated. The booking is marked `REJECTED`/cancelled in the DB (lines 607-614, 650-652) and `sendCancelledEmails` fires (line 654) while the external calendar event is still present.

The combined risk an individual reviewer would miss: this is not three unrelated `forEach(async)` typos. It is one PR-level refactor (async `getCalendar`) that systematically decoupled external-calendar mutation from the booking-lifecycle commit point across BOTH the cancellation path (`handleCancelBooking`) AND both reschedule paths (`vital`, `wipemycalother`). The invariant broken in all three is the same: 'DB state and user-facing email reflect a cancellation/reschedule that has not yet been applied to the external calendar.' A reviewer who patches one site (e.g. restores `Promise.all` in vital) is likely to ship the other two, because the sites live in unrelated modules with no shared test (per `meta_mechanical_context.json` risk_surfaces: 'Zero test coverage — 12 files across critical booking...'). The fix must be applied at all three sites AND a lint rule / `Promise.all` helper should be added to prevent the same refactor from reintroducing the pattern in the remaining `forEach(async ...)` sites the PR did not touch (`reminderScheduler.ts`, `zapier/nodeSchedulers.ts`).
findings.evidence: diff_patches for vital/lib/reschedule.ts and wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts both show: `-      bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {` -> `+      bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {` and `-            const calendar = getCalendar(...)` -> `+            const calendar = await getCalendar(...)`. diff_patches for handleCancelBooking.ts show `-        const calendar = getCalendar(calendarCredential);` -> `+        const calendar = await getCalendar(calendarCredential);` at line 449, and the forEach(async ...) at line 460 wraps the `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)` (line 467) behind `await getCalendar(credential)` (line 461). Downstream: `await apiDeletes` at line 617 and `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652; `sendCancelledEmails(evt)` at line 654. vital reschedule sends email at line 143 immediately after the forEach returns. meta_mechanical_context.json risk_surfaces: 'Zero test coverage — 12 files across critical booking...'. grep of branch shows 6 total `forEach(async` sites; 3 are in this cluster, the other 3 (reminderScheduler.ts x2, zapier/nodeSchedulers.ts x1) are not in the diff (pre-existing) but share the unguarded pattern.
findings.suggestion: Fix all three sites in one coordinated change (do not patch piecemeal): (1) vital/lib/reschedule.ts and wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts — replace `forEach(async ...)` with `const promises = bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }); await Promise.all(promises);` so deletes complete before `sendRequestRescheduleEmail`. (2) handleCancelBooking.ts lines 458-470 — replace `forEach(async (credential) => {... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)})` with `const deletePromises = credentials.filter(...).map(async (credential) => { ... return deletedEvent; }); const results = await Promise.all(deletePromises); apiDeletes.push(...results);` so `apiDeletes` is populated before being awaited at lines 617/652. (3) Add a repository lint rule (e.g. `no-async-foreach` via `eslint-plugin-no-async-foreach` or a custom rule) and/or a `Promise.all` helper wrapper for app-store iteration, so the next async-import refactor cannot reintroduce the pattern in the remaining `forEach(async ...)` sites (reminderScheduler, zapier). (4) Add integration tests covering cancellation + reschedule with a mocked calendar that asserts `deleteEvent` completed before the DB status flip and email send.
findings.title: PR's await-getCalendar-in-forEach pattern systematically defers external calendar deletes past the synchronous booking-lifecycle commit point across cancellation and reschedule flows

findings.blocking_reason: Code clarity and defensive programming suggestion; semantics are preserved and no production impact demonstrated.
findings.body: Semantics ARE preserved (verified: `await undefined` → `undefined`, guard triggers identically), but the correctness is non-obvious. findings.blocking_reason: The finding describes a missing try/catch for an edge-case chunk-load failure; the suggested fix only improves error messaging and does not itself prevent the inconsistent state, making this a defensive programming improvement rather than a demonstrated production-breaking regression.
findings.body:
Line 967: `const paymentApp = await appStore[paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName as keyof typeof appStore];`

After the PR, `appStore[key]` resolves to a `Promise` (dynamic `import()`). If the chunk fails to load (network blip, deploy race, missing chunk file during rolling deploy), `await appStore[key]` throws a `ChunkLoadError` / `TypeError: Failed to fetch dynamically imported module`. This call site is inside the `requestConfirm`/`requestReject` flow that handles **booking confirmation with refund** (`paymentInstance.refund(successPayment.id)` at line 975). An uncaught throw here:

- Aborts the entire confirm/reject mutation with a generic tRPC INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR
- Leaves the booking in an inconsistent state — the payment was already captured (successPayment exists from line ~930), but the refund never executes and the booking status is not updated to REJECTED
- The user sees a generic error with no indication that the root cause is a failed app-store chunk load

The PR narrative flags "No import-failure error handling" as a general risk surface. This finding documents the specific blast radius for this call site: a failed chunk load during booking confirmation/refund corrupts the payment+booking state machine.

Note: the pre-PR static-import version would have failed at build/module-load time (the whole module wouldn't load), so this is a newly-introduced runtime failure mode for this specific path.
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `requestConfirm`/`requestReject` handler reaches the refund block around line 940 after a successful payment exists (`successPayment.appId`).
Step 2: Line 967 `const paymentApp = await appStore[paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName as keyof typeof appStore];` — post-PR `appStore[dirName]` is `Promise<AppModule>` from `import()` in `packages/app-store/index.ts`.
Step 3: If the dynamic `import()` rejects (chunk missing, network failure), `await` rethrows inside the tRPC procedure.
Step 4: tRPC wraps uncaught errors into TRPCError (INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) and aborts the mutation. Line 975 `paymentInstance.refund(...)` and line 983 `prisma.booking.update(... REJECTED ...)` never execute.
Step 5: Result: payment stays captured, booking is not marked REJECTED, user sees generic error — inconsistent payment/booking state with no specific log indicating a chunk-load failure.
findings.title: await appStore[key] in refund flow has no try/catch — failed dynamic import throws uncaught in booking confirm/reject path

findings.blocking_reason: The finding explicitly confirms this is correct intentional deferred-await async behavior, not a bug.
findings.body: CalendarManager.getCalendarCredentials (line 23-36) calls getCalendar(credential) without await and stores the resulting Promise<Calendar | null> in item.calendar. This is intentionally deferred — the consumer getConnectedCalendars does await item.calendar at line 48. This is correct async behavior (parallel awaiting pattern), but it is being reviewed under the 'getCalendarCredentials stores Promise<Calendar>' dimension. Not a sync→async boundary bug — the promise is never used as a sync value.
findings.evidence: calls getCalendar(credential) without await and stores the resulting Promise<Calendar | null> in item.calendar
findings.title: Notable: getCalendarCredentials stores Promise<Calendar>

findings.blocking_reason: No bug exists today; this is a code-quality suggestion about adding an explicit return type annotation with no demonstrated production impact.
findings.body:
After the refactor, `getCalendar` returns `Promise<Calendar|null>` instead of `Calendar|null`. `getCalendarCredentials` (lines 23-36) is NOT async and was NOT updated to await the new promise — line 28 calls `getCalendar(credential)` and line 29 stores the result directly into the `.calendar` field of the returned object. This means the runtime type of `.calendar` silently widened from `Calendar|null` to `Promise<Calendar|null>`.

This is currently SAFE because:
1. The only consumer that accesses `.calendar` is `getConnectedCalendars` (line 48), which WAS correctly updated to `const calendar = await item.calendar;` — properly unwrapping the Promise.
2. `getConnectedCalendars` accepts `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>`, so TypeScript inference flows the widened type correctly.
3. All three external consumers (apps/web/pages/api/availability/calendar.ts:83, packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer.tsx:340 and :415) only pass the result to `getConnectedCalendars` and never access `.calendar` directly.
4. Other internal callers (getCachedResults:142, createEvent:233, updateEvent:284, deleteEvent:335) call `getCalendar` directly with `await` and bypass `getCalendarCredentials` entirely.

No bug exists today. However, the type contract change is implicit — there is no explicit return type annotation on `getCalendarCredentials`, so the widening is only visible by tracing the inferred type. A future consumer that synchronously accesses `.calendar` (e.g. `creds[0].calendar?.getTimezone()`) would silently operate on a Promise object rather than a Calendar, producing NaN/undefined instead of a type error in some cases. Adding an explicit return type annotation would make this contract change visible at the function boundary.
findings.dimension_name: Type contract change in getCalendarCredentials after getCalendar async refactor
findings.evidence: Line 28: `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` (no await). Line 29: stored directly into object. Line 35: returned without explicit type. Line 48 in getConnectedCalendars: `const calendar = await item.calendar;` proves the contract is Promise-typed and must be awaited.
findings.suggestion: Consider adding an explicit return type annotation to `getCalendarCredentials` that reflects the new Promise-typed `.calendar` field, e.g. `: { integration: string; credential: CalendarCredential; calendar: Promise<Calendar | null> }[]`. This makes the type widening visible at the function signature and prevents future consumers from accidentally treating `.calendar` as a synchronous value.
findings.title: getCalendarCredentials implicitly widens .calendar field to Promise<Calendar|null> without explicit type annotation

The widening is implicit (no explicit return type annotation on `getCalendarCredentials`), making the contract change only visible by tracing the inferred type. findings.blocking_reason: Noisy console.warn log output is a code quality issue, not a build, security, data, API, or behavior regression.
findings.body:
Line 968-970:
```ts
if (!(paymentApp && "lib" in paymentApp && "PaymentService" in paymentApp.lib)) {
  console.warn(`payment App service of type ${paymentApp} is not implemented`);
```

`${paymentApp}` stringifies the entire imported module object (which after the PR is the resolved module namespace, not `undefined`). This produces verbose, unstructured log output like `[object Object]` or a giant module dump. When `paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName` is missing/invalid, `appStore[undefined as keyof ...]` returns `undefined` and `await undefined` is `undefined`, so the warning reads `payment App service of type undefined is not implemented` — acceptable. But when the dirName is valid but the app simply lacks a `PaymentService`, the warning dumps the whole module.

This is a pre-existing issue (the same `console.warn` existed before the PR), but the PR changes what `paymentApp` evaluates to at this point (now a resolved module namespace instead of a directly-imported module), so the stringification output changes shape.
findings.evidence:
Step 1: Line 967 `const paymentApp = await appStore[...]` resolves to a module namespace object (post-PR) or undefined (if key missing).
Step 2: Line 968 the guard `!(paymentApp && "lib" in paymentApp && "PaymentService" in paymentApp.lib)` is true when the module loaded but has no PaymentService.
Step 3: Line 969 `${paymentApp}` stringifies the module namespace object — noisy and uninformative.
findings.suggestion:
Log the `dirName` instead of the module object:
```ts
console.warn(`Payment App service '${paymentAppCredential?.app?.dirName}' is not implemented`);
```
This is actionable — operators can see exactly which app directory lacks a PaymentService.
findings.title: console.warn interpolates the entire paymentApp module object — noisy log output when dirName lookup returns a module without PaymentService
